readings.title: Applying for a local permit
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents used an online form for a small street event. Many applications were returned because the required map was missing. The main obstacle was a document requirement explained too late. The form mentioned the map only after applicants had completed several pages. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a review of returned applications. Staff identified repeated omissions and watched first-time users find the document list. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated early guidance prevented repeated work. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a checklist before the first form page. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: clear procedures save time for everyone. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in applying for a local permit, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A library fine notice
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A library sent overdue notices containing several rules. Readers were unsure whether they needed to pay or simply return a book. The main obstacle was different actions mixed in one paragraph. A reminder, a charge and an appeal option appeared together without separate headings. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used a reading exercise with volunteers. Staff asked readers to identify the next action for three realistic examples. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated action headings improved understanding. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced separate notices for return, payment and questions. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: a rule is useful when people know what to do. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in a library fine notice, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Explaining a roadwork notice
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A council announced a temporary road closure. Shop owners knew the dates but did not know how customers could reach their doors. The main obstacle was notice focused on vehicles rather than access. The document named the closed street but omitted the pedestrian route and delivery arrangements. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used questions collected from affected businesses. Officers compared the planned barriers with actual entrances to shops. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated access details were essential to daily planning. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised notice with pedestrian and delivery maps. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: public notices should answer practical questions. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in explaining a roadwork notice, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A community room booking rule
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Local groups tried to reserve a community room. Some thought a provisional request was a confirmed booking. The main obstacle was unclear status after submitting a form. The automatic message thanked applicants but did not say when approval would arrive. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a check of booking messages and disputes. Staff reviewed timestamps and asked applicants what they understood from the response. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a status label would prevent double planning. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced distinct pending and confirmed messages. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: service rules need clear confirmation. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a community room booking rule, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning public services and understanding rules often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the civic information programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关公共服务与规则理解的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the civic information team proposing a small improvement to the civic information programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the civic information programme. People have noticed a document requirement explained too late, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
